paragraphs.heading: Time beyond a human life
paragraphs.text: Deep time is the idea of geological time stretching across billions of years, far past anything a person can live through. It gives scientists a frame for explaining how Earth formed and changed, how life developed, and the slow processes that reshape a planet. The modern view involves huge changes over the age of the Earth, which, after a long and tangled history of work, is put at around 4.55 billion years.

paragraphs.heading: Hutton's endless cycle
paragraphs.text: The Scottish geologist James Hutton developed the idea in the 18th century. Earlier geologists such as Nicolas Steno had pictured rock layers forming from water through chemical processes, and Abraham Gottlob Werner built this into a theory called Neptunism, in which minerals slowly crystallised in ancient oceans. Hutton's 1785 theory, based instead on Plutonism, imagined a cycle without end. Rocks form under the sea, are lifted up and tilted, then wear away to make new layers under the sea again.

paragraphs.heading: Giddy at Siccar Point
paragraphs.text: In June 1788 Hutton stood with the mathematician John Playfair and with James Hall before the rock layers at Siccar Point. What they saw there persuaded Playfair and Hall that this very slow cycle was real. Playfair remarked that his mind seemed to grow dizzy from peering so deep into time. In the same year Hutton wrote that he could see no trace of a beginning and no sign of an end.

paragraphs.heading: Sudden or slow change
paragraphs.text: During the 19th century, deep time turned from a radical notion into a basic principle of geology and of evolutionary theory. Georges Cuvier, a pioneer of paleontology, argued that Earth's past was marked by a string of catastrophes, each followed by new life forms appearing suddenly. This view, called catastrophism, saw history as broken into segments rather than running on without a break. Charles Lyell answered with uniformitarianism in his Principles of Geology (1830–1833): slow, gradual work by erosion, sedimentation and volcanoes had shaped the surface over vast periods, so Earth had to be far older than once thought.

paragraphs.heading: Time enough for evolution
paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin read Lyell's book during his voyage on HMS Beagle in the 1830s and was deeply influenced by it. Lyell's long timescale gave Darwin the room his theory of evolution by natural selection needed. Without such a vast stretch of time behind it, evolutionary change would have seemed implausible. Accepting deep time in geology therefore opened the way to new theories of how life developed and branched out.

paragraphs.heading: Learning to think in deep time
paragraphs.text: Thinkers have long tried to make such huge spans easier to grasp. Wells and Julian Huxley, writing in The Science of Life in 1929, held that moving between different scales is just a matter of practice. Like maps or microscopes, they suggested, deep time asks us to train the imagination.

paragraphs.heading: Deep time today
paragraphs.text: Deep time is now used more and more in science communication and public outreach, as a lens on human impact during the Anthropocene. The Anthropocene is a proposed new epoch of geological time, marked out by the way humans affect Earth's systems. The BBC has described how thinking about deep time can build patience, humility and long-term thinking. One podcast episode looked at nuclear waste stores, meant to stay secure for tens of thousands of years, as a real case of planning across such vast spans.
